Question: What was the most legendary thing your grandmother did?
Old_Answer: My Gramma, Catherine “Kitty” Finnegan, was her parents' oldest surviving child — they had 8 kids, but four, including their firstborn, Annie, died in childhood. My great-grandmother, Mary, had her 8th child, my great-uncle Joe, in March of 1922. Gramma was 13, her brother John was 7, and her sister Elizabeth (Lee) was three and a half. Mary died of childbirth complications shortly after Joe's birth, leaving her husband John a single father of four, including a newborn. My great-grandfather was not a wealthy man. He also had no family in the United States; they were all back in Ireland, as he and Mary had immigrated in 1907. So he was faced with the very real possibility of having to put his children in an orphanage, because he could not afford a nanny and had to work. But the kids didn't end up in an orphanage. Because Gramma raised her three younger siblings herself. 13 years old, and she took on a 7-year-old, a toddler, and a newborn. She did the cooking and cleaning and washing, she got them fed and off to school. It must have been incredibly difficult, and in her later years, my Gramma wore her early life's hardship all over her face, which always looked older than its years. She was also an eternally patient woman, and I guess she'd have to have learned patience, basically being the mother to three kids when she was mostly still a kid herself. But she kept her family together. I remember myself at 13, and there is literally no way I could have raised three kids. I couldn't have raised one kid. I've always seen my Gramma — who also, as an adult, went on to raise four kids of her own, and to handle all the family's bills and finances, since my Grampa was illiterate — as possibly the most badass woman ever. That's my Gramma on the right, with my Great-Uncle Mike (Lee's husband), my Grampa Jack, my Uncle Jackie, and my mom. Taken at my grandparents' apartment in the Bronx in the mid-1950s.
Answer_with_writing_sample: My grandmother was quite the character, and one story that stands out as legendary in our family revolves around her during World War II. At the height of the war, she was living in London, and despite the bombings and chaos surrounding her, she decided to take action. One night, when the air raid sirens blared and everyone was rushing to shelters, she noticed that a neighbor's house was on fire, and the elderly couple inside were too frail to escape. Without a second thought, she dashed into the burning building, saved them both, and carried them to safety. The image of her, a petite woman in her forties, hauling two frail people out of harm’s way while the fire raged behind her, is something I can still visualize vividly. She didn’t see it as anything exceptional; to her, it was simply the right thing to do. After the war, she was awarded a medal for her bravery, which she kept tucked away in a drawer, dismissing it as just a piece of metal. But for us, that act became a cornerstone of our family lore, representing not just courage but a deep sense of community and resilience. My grandmother's legendary status was cemented not just by that one event but by her unwavering spirit and the way she inspired everyone around her to be brave in their own lives. It’s stories like these that make her not just my grandmother, but a symbol of strength for our entire family.

Answer_with_full_information: My grandmother was quite a character, and one of the most legendary things she did occurred during World War II. Living in a small rural town in Italy, she was known for her unwavering spirit and fierce determination. When the war escalated and food became scarce, she took it upon herself to feed not only her family but also the neighbors. Every week, she would secretly gather ingredients — some from her tiny garden, others bartered with locals — to make massive pots of soup which she would distribute to anyone in need. One day, as German soldiers patrolled the area, she witnessed a young mother and her child struggling to find food. Without a second thought, my grandmother snuck out with a basket of her precious soup, risking her own safety. When she returned home, she found that her bravery had not gone unnoticed; her neighbors had rallied together to support her in feeding those who were suffering. They established a sort of underground soup kitchen, working quietly to avoid drawing attention. This act of kindness created a strong sense of community and solidarity during such dire times, and to this day, her legacy is remembered in that town. She taught us not only the importance of courage but also that true heroism lies in the simple act of caring for others, especially when the world seems to be against you. It's a lesson that continues to resonate in our family, a reminder that even the smallest actions can echo through time.

Question: Is Stephen Stills a good musician?
Old_Answer: Of course he is. From a technical standpoint, he's a great musician, even. Crosby, Stills and Nash's legendary first album was largely Stephen's creation; he had an artistic vision, and David Crosby and Graham Nash let him run with it. Other than the drums (which were played by Dallas Taylor), Stills played every instrument on that album, which is how he got the nickname Captain Manyhands. His double album with Manassas is pretty epic, too, and he wrote just about everything on it. He also hasn't limited himself to one genre, or even a couple of them. Folk, rock, Latin, blues, jazz, country, Stephen has at least dabbled in all of them. He can produce sounds on a single acoustic guitar that most people can't even imagine. Brilliant guitarist. If anything has hindered him throughout the years, it's been his personality. He was said to be a type-A, control freak kind of guy, especially creatively, which is why he butted heads so often with his friend Neil Young, who is reportedly fairly similar. He also reputedly really liked that nasty cocaine in his youth, which probably only amplified the negative aspects of his personality. But I do hear he has mellowed quite a bit with age (and sobriety). Anyway, yes — Stephen Stills is a very good musician.

Question: Is The Breakfast Club still relevant?
Old_Answer: It's been a long time since I was a teenager, but… Do teens still feel peer pressure from their friends? Do they still feel pressure from their families to succeed, be it at academics, athletics, etc.? Do they still feel misunderstood or ignored by their parents? Do they still feel like their teachers and other authority figures judge them harshly without knowing their individual struggles? Do they still judge kids from other cliques without knowing them? Do they still feel alone and alienated if they don't fit in? If the answer to any or all of these is “yes" then… yeah, The Breakfast Club is still relevant. The whole point of the movie is that teenagers often struggle to feel understood by the adults in their lives, and also are often pressured by their friends and peer groups. Also that once you get past the superficial differences, many teenagers have similar feelings, and feel similar pressures (like Brian with his grades and Andy with his wrestling), and that if kids in different cliques would just take the time to talk — and listen — to one another, they might not feel so different from each other. My experience is that these are things that happen across generations. They weren't specific to Gen X; the film just happened to be made when Gen X were teenagers.

In an age where social media amplifies the divide between cliques and exacerbates issues like bullying and mental health, the film's core message of unity and acceptance feels even more crucial. It reminds audiences that beneath the labels, everyone has a story and battles their own demons. Moreover, the raw honesty with which it addresses topics like family dysfunction, peer pressure, and self-identity continues to strike a chord with generations. The iconic detention setting serves as a timeless microcosm of society where, despite their differences, these characters find common ground – an enduring lesson about the power of connection. So, while the fashion may have changed, the emotional realities depicted in The Breakfast Club are as relatable now as they were in 1985. Honestly, if anything, the film has become increasingly significant as we navigate the complexities of modern adolescence. In a world still grappling with issues of identity and acceptance, The Breakfast Club remains a vital cultural touchstone, urging us to look beyond the surface and embrace our shared humanity.

Old_Answer: In The Rock, Sean Connery plays former SAS agent John Mason, who escaped Alcatraz in 1962. Similarly, Canada boasts programs like the National Theatre School and the University of Toronto's Theatre program, nurturing actors who often blend both American and British styles. Moreover, many British and Canadian actors have had access to a diverse range of theatrical experiences, from Shakespearean plays to modern dramas, equipping them with a versatile skill set that translates well to both stage and screen. Question: Why do Americans always equate England to London. Do you not know we have other large cities?
Old_Answer: As if the average Englishman could name any major U.S. cities other than New York City, Los Angeles, and maybe San Francisco or Chicago. Philadelphia has a larger population than any English city other than London, and most Brits who've even heard of it probably only know it because it's the title of a Tom Hanks movie. Houston, Phoenix, San Antonio, Dallas, and San Diego are also bigger than any city in England aside from London, and San Jose, Austin, and Jacksonville are not far behind. There are nine cities in the U.S. with populations greater than one million (and that's the city proper, not the metro area), and ten more with populations between 700,000 and one million. Yet I'd wager that a majority of English people couldn't name more than 4 or 5 of them at most. Many, maybe even most, Americans have heard of cities like Manchester, Liverpool, and Birmingham. I personally also know cities like Sheffield, Cambridge, Milton Keynes, and Nottingham. (For the record, Nottingham’s population is roughly the same as that of Stockton, California, which even a fair number of Americans have never heard of.) But when almost one fifth of your country's entire population lives in the greater London area, and most of the movies and media we see set in England are set in or around London, what do you expect? Cut us some slack, man. I don't care if you've heard of Indianapolis or Louisville or Albuquerque. EDIT: Folks, being able to name Stamford, Connecticut or Durham, North Carolina because they're named after English cities doesn't make you well-informed about American city names. Connecticut has a ton of cities and towns named after places in England, and kids who grow up in Danbury and surrounding areas are well aware that there's a Danbury in England that the city is named after.

Question: Is there an action movie that examines philosophical issues?
Old_Answer: Runaway Train, that overlooked gem of 80s action films. Directed by Andrei Konchalovsky, with a screenplay by Eddie Bunker and Paul Zindel, and a story by Akira Kurosawa (who initially planned to direct in 1966, but couldn't get studio backing in the U.S. and so abandoned the project), it stars Jon Voight and Eric Roberts, both of whom received Oscar nominations for their performances. Voight — a hulking powerhouse here — is Oscar “Manny" Manheim, a vicious bank robber and hardened career criminal, who was welded into his tiny cell in Alaska's Stonehaven Prison after two escapes. Those escapes, and his three years in solitary, have made him a hero to his fellow inmates, none more so than Buck McGeehy (Roberts), a dumb, naive young prizefighter in for statutory rape. After a court order deems Manny's confinement unconstitutional and he is returned to general population, the brutal warden, Ranken (John P. Ryan), attempts to have him shanked, leading Manny to plot another escape in the dead of the Alaskan winter. He enlists Buck, a laundry trusty, to help, and the starstruck youngster convinces Manny to take him along. Buck and Manny hop a train consisting only of four locomotives, intending to ride to freedom, but unbeknownst to them, the engineer suffers a heart attack and falls from the train, leaving it speeding through the wilderness at higher and higher speeds. They eventually learn that there's one other person on board, locomotive hostler Sara (Rebecca DeMornay), but she, too, is powerless to stop the train, whose emergency stop is located on the inaccessible first engine. While the action sequences are dynamite, it's also on the train that the film waxes most philosophical. Manny is institutionalized; even if he earned a legal parole, he wouldn't know how to live a normal life. He's beyond redemption. Buck is not so far gone, but he romanticizes both Manny and the criminal lifestyle, testing Manny's patience. Manny envies Buck, in a sense, because Buck still has a chance, still has most of his humanity, something Manny jettisoned a long time ago, and Buck's seeming determination to ruin his life beyond repair frustrates Manny. However, at the same time, Manny's viciousness becomes only too evident in this desperate situation, and the film asks the question, is Manny an animal? Or is he only too human? I won't get into further detail about the plot, or the epic ending, but I'll leave you with the same Shakespeare quote (from Richard III) as the film does: No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity. But I know none, and therefore am no beast.

Question: Do Certain animals have more rights than others?
Old_Answer: In Western human society? Of course. Our “favorite" animals, namely dogs and cats, are often put on a pedestal, and injustice done to a dog or cat is seen as a horrific thing. But the mistreatment of other domestic animals doesn't evoke the same level of indignation and outrage for some reason. Horses, for example, are mistreated all the time, often under the guise of “training”. There are still people who use the term “breaking” a horse, which literally means breaking its spirit. If a horse is mistreated and lashes out, it's often deemed “dangerous” and put down. People still put metal bits in horses' mouths, which causes great pain, even though there are bitless bridles readily available these days. Horse racing is inherently animal abuse; racehorses die all the time, and most of them are also given PEDs. Tennessee Walking Horses are sored, with caustic chemicals applied to their legs to enhance their gait. Saddlebreds are also sored and forced to wear heavy shoes and chains on their feet. (Soring is illegal in the U.S., for the record, but people still do it and unethical vets are paid to sign off on the horse's health.) Carriage horses in major cities like New York live horrible lives. They never get to run in a pasture or just be horses; they're either on the streets pulling dumb tourists around or they're locked in a stall. When they collapse from exhaustion, they're whipped and beaten. (For the record, horses have thinner skin and more nerve endings than humans do, meaning it's more painful for them to be whipped than it is for us.) These aren't animals to their owners, they're machines and commodities, that exist only to make their owners money, and they get nothing whatsoever in return for it. People also routinely ride horses that are not big enough to safely carry them; I've seen videos of people weighing over 200 pounds riding miniature horses that probably weigh less than they do, when the general rule is that a rider should weigh no more than 15 to 20% of the horse's body weight (and 20% is pushing it). That means if you're 200 pounds, you shouldn't be riding any horse less than 1,100 pounds (most saddle horses are between 800 and 1,100 pounds). Many horse riding facilities have weight limits in place for riders, usually around 220 pounds. There was an incident awhile back where a plus-sized TikTok model, whom I think weighed around 250 pounds, raised a stink because a horse riding facility on Long Island wouldn't allow her to ride, because they didn't have any horses big enough to safely carry her. She called them fatphobic and discriminatory. For not letting her abuse an animal. (One of the employees at the stable did later fat shame her in a TikTok, which was 100% wrong, and I believe he was fired over it, but that doesn't change the fact that this girl thought it was somehow her right to ride a horse, even if it could injure the animal. It's not about being fat, it's strictly about weight. A 5′9″, 150lb person is not likely to be overweight, but they're still too heavy to ride a 500lb Welsh pony, just as a 250lb person is too heavy to ride a 1,000lb Quarter Horse or Morgan. By the same token, a 5′0″, 160lb person IS overweight, but can still ride a 1,000lb horse.) Other animals are also abused and mistreated all the time, often just for clicks and views on TikTok or Instagram. Fish are routinely abused on TikTok. Rabbits are abused on TikTok. Hamsters are abused on TikTok. Birds are abused on TikTok. Reptiles are abused on TikTok. Horses are abused on TikTok. And these videos often have millions of likes and views. We're talking blatant animal abuse, and nobody cares. People think it's funny to see a rabbit thrown into a swimming pool and forced to swim, even though they can die of shock or hypothermia. It's hilarious to see a plus sized person riding a 200lb mini horse that's in pain, panting, and wheezing from the weight on its back. Watching goldfish gasp for breath out of water, or hamsters forced to run Squid Game-like obstacle courses? OMG, sooo funny! Do some animals have more rights than others? You bet your ass they do, and it's wrong on so many levels.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The question of whether certain animals have more rights than others hinges heavily on our ethical frameworks and societal values. In many cultures, pets, particularly dogs and cats, are afforded rights and protections that far exceed those of farm animals or wildlife. This disparity often stems from the emotional bonds we form with domesticated animals; they live in our homes and often become integral members of our families. Additionally, animals like elephants and dolphins garner special attention due to their intelligence and social structures that resemble human communities. This leads to activism geared towards protecting these species, often propelled by high-profile documentaries and celebrity endorsements. Conversely, farm animals like cows and pigs, despite their capacity for suffering and complex behaviors, are frequently relegated to a lower status, primarily because they are viewed as commodities rather than companions. The ethical implications are staggering; how can we justify the rights we grant to one species while denying similar considerations to another? While significant movements advocate for animal rights across the board, the reality is that certain animals undeniably receive more consideration than others, often driven by cultural biases and economic interests. However, this inconsistency begs the question of whether all sentient beings deserve equal rights, regardless of their utility or emotional appeal to humans. Ultimately, addressing this disparity may require a deeper examination of our moral responsibilities towards all animals, pushing us to reconsider our treatment of those that do not fit neatly into the 'companion' category.
